div.head: Wl art 4
div.ab: Et omnis Francigena qui tempore regis Eadwardi, propinqui mei, fuit in Anglia particeps consuetudinum Anglorum, quod ipsi dicunt on hlóte et an scóte, persoluatur secundum legem Anglorum. Hoc decretum sancitum est in Ciuitate Claudia.

Et omnis Francigena qui, tempore regis Eadwardi propinqui mei, fuit in Anglia particeps consuetudinum Anglorum, quod ipsi dicunt on hlóte et an scóte, persolvatur secundum legem Anglorum. Hoc decretum sancitum est in Civitate Claudia.

But every Frenchman who, in the time of King Edward, my kinsman, was admitted to the status of an Englishman, which they call being "in lot and in scot," shall be paid for according to English law. This decree was enacted at Gloucester.
div.note: Added October 2026 from Robertson pp. 238–239 (text and translation); Liebermann’s text added from Gesetze I p. 487, October 2026 (two independent readings of the page images)

note.seg: so (min mæg) heisst Eadward III. in Wilhelms I. Kanzleistil (auch Leis Wl., Prol.) als Enkel Richards I., dessen Urenkel Wilhelm war. Vielleicht liegt hier sogar Wilhelms Sprache vor
thus (min mæg) Eadward III is called in William I’s chancery style (also Leis Wl., Prol.), as grandson of Richard I, whose great-grandson William was. Perhaps we even have William’s own language here

sonst bezeichnet die Phrase nur Bürgerrecht in einer Ortsgemeinde. Dachte Wilhelm zunächst an städtische Einwanderer (z. B. Londons und Winchesters)? Oder führte nur der Compilator irrig scot ein (wie lot zu Hn Lond 2, 1 interpolirt ward)?

elsewhere the phrase denotes only the rights of a burgess in a local community. Was William thinking first of immigrants to the towns (e.g. of London and Winchester)? Or did only the compiler erroneously introduce scot (as lot was interpolated in Hn Lond 2, 1)?

pcrsolvat, die Verderbnis der Tripartita, wird von Round (Domesday stud. I 125) und Cunningham (Growth of industry 178. 312) wohl richtig so erklärt: der vor 1066 Naturalisierte zahle auch ferner Englische Steuer, obwohl Francigenae mit masurae, die früher Bodenlast trugen, seit 1067 sich in Cambridge und Shrewsbury dem Beitrage zur städtischen Staatssteuer entziehen; Domesday I 189a 1. 252a 1

pcrsolvat, the corruption of the Tripartita, is probably rightly explained by Round (Domesday stud. I 125) and Cunningham (Growth of industry 178. 312) as follows: the man naturalized before 1066 was to continue paying English tax, although from 1067 Francigenae with masurae that had formerly borne a burden on the land withdrew from contributing to the borough’s share of the national tax in Cambridge and Shrewsbury; Domesday I 189a 1. 252a 1
